lessons.title: A small plan for a feeling
lessons.outcome: Create art linked to an emotion (links PSHE).
lessons.goal: I can plan a small piece about a feeling.
success: I can choose a feeling for a made-up piece.
I can try two ways and choose one.
I can plan a start and an end.
words: A feeling, such as joy, calm or worry.
An idea for what you will make.

stages.name: Arrival
pupil: You can point, speak, sign or pass.
Our art can be about a made-up person.
Pick joy, calm or worry. You may choose your own word.
stages.say: An emotion is a feeling. Our art can show a feeling in an invented story. A made-up person might wait for a turn, get help or hear good news. Pick one feeling for your piece. You do not need to tell us about your own life. You may work quietly and show me in private.
stages.good: The pupil chooses or confirms an emotion for an invented piece. The adult accepts a pupil's own word without asking for personal history.
stages.fallback: Name two choices slowly. A pupil can point, sign, direct an adult or indicate a choice with an agreed gesture.
stages.answer: Joy, calm, worry or another pupil-chosen feeling is valid. An adult may explain the word but does not decide what the pupil must feel.

stages.name: Starter
pupil: A made-up person waits for a turn.
What might they feel? More than one idea can fit.
Which marks or moves could show your idea?
stages.say: Our made-up person waits for a turn. They might feel calm, glad, unsure or cross. We do not know until the maker tells us. Show one line, quiet tap or silent move that could fit your idea.
stages.good: The pupil offers an emotion and one possible artistic feature. Different readings of the same fictional situation are accepted.
stages.fallback: The adult shows a smooth hand path and a short zigzag path. The pupil chooses one, directs a new path or describes it in words.
stages.answer: For example, a still hand could show calm or waiting. A quick zigzag could show worry or excitement. Ask the maker for the intended meaning rather than marking one feeling correct.

stages.name: I do
pupil: Watch two tests for the same feeling.
Paint: try a curve, then a short zigzag.
Sound: try soft slow taps, then soft quick taps.
Choose one way to work. Plan a start and an end.
stages.say: My invented piece is about hope while waiting. I touch the brush lightly to scrap paper and pull a short curve. I try a zigzag beside it. I choose the curve because it seems to open out. My small painting will start with one curve and end with three spaced curves. If I choose sound, I test four slow soft taps, then four quicker soft taps. I choose slow taps, a pause, then the same taps again. I keep the volume low. I am planning an order, not just choosing a colour. These are adult examples, not rules for your work.
stages.good: The adult shows two small tests and links a choice to an intended emotion. The plan states a beginning and an ending. A sound plan names the actions in order, so the pupil can return to it next lesson.
stages.fallback: Use an air drawing or silent finger moves. Show the beginning, pause and ending with the hands. A pupil may direct the adult instead of making the movement.
stages.answer: Ask: 'Have I chosen a feeling and an order, or only picked a tool?' Expected: a feeling and an order. If unclear, point to the beginning and ending, then ask the pupil to choose what comes first.

stages.name: We do
pupil: Choose one feeling for a class piece.
Try two small versions. Say what changed.
Choose the first part and the last part.
Finish: We chose ___ because ___.
stages.say: You choose the emotion for our invented piece. I will make two versions while keeping the tool or volume the same. Tell me which marks or pace fit your idea. Then direct the start and end. Hinge: Which helps us return to the idea tomorrow: A keep only a colour word, or B keep the feeling, chosen marks or actions, and their order?
stages.good: Each pupil makes or confirms a choice. Pupils compare a controlled change, such as curve versus zigzag or slow versus quick, and identify a useful ordered plan. The shared class model stays separate from individual evidence.
stages.fallback: Pupils direct two silent hand sequences. The adult repeats their chosen start and end, then reads the oral plan back for confirmation.
stages.answer: B keeps the feeling, action and order. If a pupil chooses A, model that the same colour could make many different pieces. Parallel check: 'Which reminder helps with sound: quiet, or four soft taps, pause, four taps?' Continue when the pupil identifies the ordered reminder.

stages.name: Create
pupil: In your book or arts log, choose a feeling.
Try two small marks, sounds or silent moves.
Choose one way. Make a tiny trial piece.
Plan your start and end for next time.
Keep your tests and say why you chose them.
stages.say: Choose paint, original sound or a silent route. For paint, use a small amount on the brush tip and test on scrap. Keep paint and water on the mat. Rinse and wipe the brush before a new colour. For sound, use four gentle fingertip taps and a pause, below talking volume. Stop on my raised hand. Change only the mark shape or pace in your two tests so you can notice its effect. Choose the version for your piece and try a tiny ordered version. In the log, keep a small plan or spoken sequence for tomorrow. A pupil may direct an adult's hands and materials.
stages.good: Two real tests, a small original trial and a plan with a start and end. The pupil names the intended feeling and gives a feature-based reason. The plan is manageable for the next 40 minute lesson. A test may stay unfinished if the log records its true state.
stages.fallback: Use a silent hand sequence or an air drawing, or direct the adult. Confirm an ordered plan aloud. The adult records the pupil's actual sequence, emotion and reason at the next available recording opportunity. Art materials and a device are not needed for participation.
stages.answer: Example only: a hopeful piece starts with one small curve and ends with three open curves. A quiet sound version begins with four slow taps, pauses, then repeats. A pupil may choose a different pattern and explain it. Do not substitute this adult example for pupil evidence.

stages.name: Review
pupil: Show your trial to an adult or partner.
Say: My piece is about ___.
Say: I chose ___ because ___.
Tidy and keep your plan for next time.
stages.say: The maker explains the emotion. The listener says one thing they notice, such as a gap, a curve or a pause. The listener can read it differently. Ask the maker before touching the work. Use the final two minutes to cap paint, wipe mats and put the work flat to dry. Keep each pupil's own tests and ordered plan together.
stages.good: A real feature is noticed and the pupil's intention remains their own. Tests, trial and plan are safely stored. Private sharing is equally acceptable.
stages.fallback: The pupil directs a repeat of their silent sequence to the adult. The adult describes one observed feature and confirms the intended emotion with the pupil.
stages.answer: A useful comment is 'I notice the last curves have more space.' Do not infer a private event or tell the maker what they must feel.

stages.name: Exit
pupil: Arts log: My piece is about ___.
I chose ___ because ___.
First I will ___. At the end I will ___.
Keep your real test or a note of what you did.
stages.say: Tell me the feeling, one choice and the order for next time. You can draw, speak, sign or point. I can write your own words, read them back and let you correct them. We keep the actual date and support used. This plan helps tomorrow's making.
stages.good: A dated arts-log entry links the pupil's emotion, chosen feature, reason and ordered plan to the real trial. A witness note describes what was actually seen or heard.
stages.fallback: Confirm the feeling and ordered sequence orally. The adult keeps a short witnessed note when a recording method is available, with the actual date and support.
stages.answer: Example only: My piece is about hope. I chose curves because they seem open. First I will make one small curve. At the end I will make three curves.

Supported: Pick a feeling, or point to your own word.
Try two marks or moves with an adult.
Choose one. Make a tiny test piece.
Point to your start and end. Tell the adult your reason.
Independent: Choose a feeling for an invented piece.
Try two ways. Keep both tests.
Make a tiny trial with a start and an end.
Keep your plan and reason in your arts log.
Aspire: Try one small change in the last part.
Say how it changes the effect.
Choose the end that best fits your idea.

misconceptions: The maker must tell a real personal story
Use an invented person or an abstract idea. A pupil can pass on public sharing and explain privately.
Choosing a colour is a complete plan
Add the mark or action and the beginning and ending. A short spoken sequence is a valid plan.
A feeling has one correct colour or pace
Ask the maker for their intention. Accept a different interpretation when it links a feature to a reason.
kit: For four pupils: four books or arts logs, four pencils and eight small scrap pieces for two tests each.

Paint route: four small trial sheets, five brushes including the adult model, four mats, two stable water pots, a small shared amount of washable paint and cloths. Use familiar materials and check access needs.
Sound route: fingertips or soft knee taps only if comfortable. No instrument or recorded sound is needed. Provide a silent option.
Adult model: two tiny tests and a short ordered plan. Keep four labelled trays or safe spaces for individual work and a flat drying space.
Materials-free route: silent hand patterns, air drawing or pupil-directed adult movement. Record an oral plan when paper becomes available.
demo: 0 to 15 seconds
Say: My invented piece is about hope. Touch the brush lightly to scrap and pull a short curve. Or trace it in the air.
15 to 30 seconds
Try a zigzag beside the curve. Say: I choose the curve because it seems open. These are my two tests.
30 to 45 seconds
Show one curve at the start and three spaced curves at the end. For sound, tap four soft slow beats, pause, then repeat. Say: My plan has an order.
45 to 60 seconds
Point to the trial and plan. Say: I keep my feeling, choice and reason. Tomorrow I will use this plan to make my piece.
models: Teacher model only: My piece is about hope. I tried curves and zigzags. I chose curves because they seem open. My piece starts with one curve and ends with three.
Teacher model only: My invented person feels calm while waiting. I chose four soft slow taps, a pause, then the same taps again. I will keep that order.

lessons.title: Making my emotion piece
lessons.outcome: Create art linked to an emotion (links PSHE).
lessons.goal: I can make a small piece linked to a feeling.
success: I can use my plan to make a piece.
I can show a start and an end.
I can say how one choice fits my feeling.
words: A feeling, such as joy, calm or worry.
Which part comes first, next and last.
Look or listen again and say what you notice.

stages.name: Arrival
pupil: Find your real trial and plan.
Point to the feeling, start and end.
If you were away, make a small plan today.
stages.say: Find your own trial and plan from yesterday. Tell or show me the emotion, first part and last part. If a plan is missing or you were away, choose a feeling and make a short trial now. We record today's date and do not invent an earlier test.
stages.good: The pupil identifies their actual plan or makes an honest short restart. The intended emotion and order are clear enough for a manageable piece.
stages.fallback: The adult reads back only a witnessed prior sequence. If no record exists, offer two silent patterns and let the pupil choose and plan one now.
stages.answer: A fresh plan is valid. Keep the date and reason for the restart honest. A pupil may change the plan if they can show the new choice.

stages.name: Starter
pupil: Watch a start, a pause and an end.
Watch the end first, then the start.
What changed? Which order fits your idea?
stages.say: I show one small air curve, pause, then three open curves. Now I reverse the order. The same parts can feel different in a new order. Which order might fit hope, calm or another feeling? Explain your own reading.
stages.good: The pupil notices that the order changed and links a chosen order to an intention. No feeling is treated as a fixed answer.
stages.fallback: Use seated finger movements or describe 'one curve, then three curves'. A pupil can direct the order without moving.
stages.answer: The parts are the same but their order changed. Growing from one mark to three might suggest hope to one maker; another reading is valid with a reason.

stages.name: I do
pupil: Watch a plan become a small piece.
Make the start. Leave a space or pause.
Make the end. Check the chosen feeling.
Keep or change one part for a reason.
stages.say: My plan says hope: one small curve, then three open curves. On the left I make the first curve. I leave space, then make the ending on the right. I look back at the plan. I can keep this ending or change the space if that helps my idea. In sound, I perform four soft slow taps, pause, then repeat, and stop. I keep a simple action plan so the work can be described. This is an adult model.
stages.good: The adult uses the real model plan to make a coherent small piece with an identifiable beginning and ending. A keep or change decision links to the intended emotion, not only to neatness.
stages.fallback: Perform or direct a silent hand sequence with a clear beginning and ending. The adult can describe the ordered actions without needing a recording device.
stages.answer: Ask: 'Did my piece use my chosen order?' If unclear, point to the two planned parts and match them to the actual piece before moving on.

stages.name: We do
pupil: Help make one small class piece.
Check its start and end against the plan.
Say one part to keep or change.
The maker makes the final choice.
stages.say: You direct our class piece for a made-up person. I will follow the chosen order. Tell me what you notice before offering a change. Hinge: A listener reads the piece differently. Must the maker A change it at once, or B hear the idea and then choose for their own purpose?
stages.good: The pupil checks the work against the plan and makes a reasoned keep or change decision. The pupil understands that feedback can inform a choice while the maker keeps control.
stages.fallback: Direct the adult through a silent sequence. Use an agreed gesture to choose keep or change. The adult confirms the pupil's reason in their own words.
stages.answer: B. The maker can listen, then keep or change a feature for a reason. If unclear, model two different readings of the same curve. Parallel check: 'Can the maker keep the curve and explain why?' Expected: yes. Return to individual making when the pupil can choose a feature and a reason.

stages.name: Create
pupil: In your book or arts log, find your plan.
Make your small painting, sound or silent piece.
Give it a clear start and end.
Check one part. Keep or change it and say why.
Keep your work and your own words.
stages.say: Make a piece small enough for this lesson. Use your planned order or record a new choice. With paint, use a small amount, keep water on the mat, and rinse and wipe the brush before a new colour. Let wet marks dry before painting over them. With sound, use gentle taps below talking volume and stop on my raised hand. You may practise quietly before showing me. Check one feature, such as space, mark shape, pace or pause. Keep it or change it for a reason linked to the emotion. An adult may handle materials under your direction.
stages.good: An original emotion-linked piece with a deliberate beginning and ending, a pupil-owned choice and a brief review. If unfinished, retain the real stage and next step rather than naming it finished. A sound or movement piece may be brief and still complete for the lesson.
stages.fallback: Make or direct a silent hand piece or air drawing with a beginning and ending. The adult records the observed order and the pupil's confirmed emotion, choice and review when a recording method is available. No art materials, instrument or device is required for participation.
stages.answer: Example only: the pupil keeps a gap between two parts because it suggests waiting to them. Another pupil may remove a gap to show joy. Both are valid purposeful choices.

stages.name: Review
pupil: Share with an adult or a partner.
Say: My piece is about ___.
Show how one part fits your feeling.
Tidy and keep your piece with your log.
stages.say: The listener describes one feature before asking the maker about the intention. The maker says what they chose and why. You may share privately or pass on a public performance. Use the final two minutes to cap paint, wipe mats and store work flat. Sound and movement pupils keep their sequence plan or dated witness note beside their log.
stages.good: The pupil links a real feature to the intended emotion and hears a respectful observation. Actual work, plan and review remain together. Interpretation belongs to the maker.
stages.fallback: The adult witnesses a silent sequence privately and reads a short description back for the pupil to confirm or correct.
stages.answer: Useful review: 'My piece is about calm. I kept the slow pace because it feels still to me.' Avoid judging a pupil's private emotional state from the work.

stages.name: Exit
pupil: Arts log: I made ___.
My piece is about ___.
I kept or changed ___ because ___.
Next I would like to ___.
stages.say: Show the actual piece, plan or witnessed sequence that your words refer to. Say what you kept or changed and why. I can scribe your words, read them back and let you correct them. Record the real date, whether the piece is finished or a first version, and the help used. This entry contributes to the ongoing Explore log.
stages.good: A dated entry identifies the emotion-linked piece and a specific artistic decision. It distinguishes pupil explanation from adult observation and records the true state of the work.
stages.fallback: The pupil confirms the feeling, sequence and decision by gesture or speech. The adult makes an accurate dated observation note at the next recording opportunity.
stages.answer: Example only: I made a small painting about hope. I kept the open curves because they seem to grow. Next I would like to try longer marks.

Supported: Find your plan or make a short one now.
Make the first part, then the last part.
Point to a choice. Tell or show why you kept it.
Independent: Use your plan to make a small piece.
Give it a clear start and end.
Check one part. Keep or change it for a reason.
Add your real work and words to the arts log.
Aspire: Complete your small piece and review.
Try the end in one new way.
Which end fits your feeling best? Say why.
Keep both tests and your final choice.

log: My piece starts with ___ and ends with ___.
My work or witness note is ___.
misconceptions: A listener's different reading makes the piece wrong
The listener describes a feature. The maker explains the intention and decides whether to change anything.
More paint or louder sound makes a stronger piece
A small clear choice can work. Keep sound gentle and use a little paint; change pace, space or order instead.
A piece must be finished to keep a log entry
Record the actual stage honestly, with a next step. A first version or witnessed silent sequence can show genuine learning.
kit: For four pupils: four real trials and plans, four books or arts logs and four pencils. Have eight scrap pieces for honest catch-up trials or one changed ending.
Paint route: four small sheets, five brushes including the adult model, four mats, two stable water pots, familiar washable paint and cloths. Keep wet materials away from electrical items.
Sound route: quiet fingertips or comfortable soft knee taps, no instrument or recording device required. Offer a quiet practice space and a silent route.
Adult model: the actual short plan and a small piece made from it. Keep four individual storage places and a flat drying space.
Materials-free route: silent hand sequence, air drawing or pupil-directed adult performance. Keep a dated observed sequence and the pupil's confirmed words when recording is available.
demo: 0 to 15 seconds
Show the actual model plan. Say: My piece is about hope. My plan starts with one curve and ends with three.
15 to 30 seconds
Make the first curve with a light brush touch or in the air. Leave a gap. Say: I follow my chosen order.
30 to 45 seconds
Add the three ending curves. Or perform four soft slow taps, pause, then repeat and stop. Say: My piece has a start and an end.
45 to 60 seconds
Point to one chosen feature. Say: I keep the space because it fits my idea. I keep my real work and review together.
models: Teacher model only: I made a small painting about hope. It starts with one curve and ends with three open curves. I kept the gap because it seems like waiting.
Teacher model only: My quiet sound piece is about calm. It starts with four slow taps. After a pause I repeat them. I kept the soft pace because it feels still to me.

lessons.title: One skill to practise
lessons.outcome: Develop a skill and record it in my arts log.
lessons.goal: I can choose one technique, keep a first try and practise it.
success: I can choose one technique to practise.
I can keep a real before test and set one goal.
I can record what I tried and what I noticed.
words: A way of using a skill.
The space or time between two things.
Look or listen for what stayed the same and what changed.

stages.name: Arrival
pupil: Choose four marks or four quiet or silent actions.
Keep this choice for both lessons. You may share privately.
stages.say: Today you will choose one small technique to practise across both lessons. You could place four similar marks with even gaps, or make four quiet taps or silent finger actions at a steady pace. Pick a comfortable version. You may direct me and share privately. Before the first test, agree a neutral cue such as a slow count, or no cue. Keep the same cue and support for both tests.
stages.good: The pupil chooses or confirms one form and technique. Staff note the choice before any teaching of the method. The quiet option and stop signal are clear.
stages.fallback: Use four small silent finger actions or let the pupil direct the adult's actions. If movement is not comfortable, the pupil may direct an original four-part spoken sequence.
stages.answer: There is no best form. The important choice is one manageable technique that can be used in both periods.

stages.name: Starter
pupil: Make your first test before the adult teaches the skill.
Use four marks or four actions. Keep a note of this first try.
stages.say: This is your before test. Make four marks or four actions in your chosen way. I will not show a method yet. We will keep what really happens. If I help with materials, I will note that help. It is fine if this first try already works well. Use the cue agreed before this test, or no cue if that was the choice. I will not coach the target feature yet.
stages.good: A real four-part baseline is retained before modelling. For marks, keep the actual row and describe its gaps. For actions, record the ordered pattern and whether the three intervals seemed steady or varied. Do not judge a pupil's feeling.
stages.fallback: Adult witnesses the pupil's four silent actions or follows the pupil's four directions. Keep a dated note of the sequence, cue and actual support when a recording surface is available.
stages.answer: The first test is evidence of a starting point, not a failure. Do not replace it with a class model or claim exact timing without measuring it.

stages.name: I do
pupil: Watch the adult choose one small goal.
See how a guide or slow count can help.
The teacher model is not your before test.
stages.say: My goal is even gaps. I keep the same simple mark. I look at a gap, leave a similar gap, then make the next mark. I stop after four. For a steady action pattern I use a slow count, one, two, three, four, and make one small action on each count. I keep the same cue for practice and later tests. These are adult models.
stages.good: The adult shows a simple repeatable method and one target: roughly even spaces for marks or a steady interval for actions. The pupil identifies the target and does not need to copy the adult's design.
stages.fallback: Model the four-part method through quiet speech or comfortable silent gestures. A pupil can direct the adult. Use the same cue agreed for the pupil's chosen technique.
stages.answer: Check: Is the target A add as many marks as possible, B control the gaps or pace, or C make a perfect picture? B. If unclear, show two short rows or patterns and name only the chosen feature.

stages.name: We do
pupil: Practise the method with an adult or partner.
Change one thing at a time.
Choose your own goal for the next try.
stages.say: Let us use one simple cue. Keep the same mark or action. Try four parts, pause and notice the gaps or pace. Which one thing will you practise? Hinge: our target is even gaps. Should we A change the colour and size at once, B keep the mark and practise its gaps, or C add more marks so the row looks busy? Tell me why.
stages.good: The pupil selects B and identifies the feature to practise. An adult may model one step, then return the next action to the pupil. Each pupil has their own goal rather than a copied group answer.
stages.fallback: Use four silent actions with one slow cue. The pupil may direct the adult. Point to or say A, B or C. No sound or art materials are needed.
stages.answer: If the pupil chooses A or C, show only the target feature and ask a parallel question: For a steady four-action pattern, should we keep the cue the same or change the speed each time? Keep it the same. Continue when the pupil identifies one focused target.

stages.name: Create
pupil: Use your chosen technique. Keep the same four-part test.
Practise in two short rounds, with a pause between.
Keep your first test. Note your cue and one goal.
stages.say: Use your before record to choose one target. Practise a short round, pause, notice, then practise again. You may use more space for practice, but keep the four-part test for comparison. Record the cue, size or pace guide and any adult help. You will use the same technique in the next lesson. A pause is part of practice.
stages.good: The pupil practises the chosen technique, retains the baseline and records a specific target and cue. Staff can identify the chosen feature and what help was used. A practice round is labelled as practice, not an invented final result.
stages.fallback: Use a silent four-action sequence or pupil-directed adult sequence. Adult retains a precise dated witness note of the before test, chosen cue, practice and pupil view. A device is not needed.
stages.answer: Examples of a clear goal: I will leave similar gaps between four marks. I will keep a steady pace for four small actions. Accept a comfortable adapted version.

stages.name: Review
pupil: Show your first test and one practice try.
Say what you notice. It may be the same.
Keep your work and cue for next time.
stages.say: Compare the real records. What stayed the same? What changed? You can say that you need more practice. A partner can notice one feature without ranking the work. In the final two minutes, put tools away, keep paintings flat and store the baseline and cue together.
stages.good: The pupil makes a specific observation about gaps or pace and retains their own starting point. No improvement is assumed. Private sharing is enough. The next-period cue is clear.
stages.fallback: An adult repeats the witnessed sequence from the note and asks the pupil to confirm it. Keep staff observations distinct from the pupil's words.
stages.answer: Useful: The gap after mark two is smaller. The first three actions were steady and the last came sooner. Vague praise alone is not the comparison.

stages.name: Exit
pupil: Arts log: My technique is ___.
My first try showed ___. My goal is ___.
Next time I will use the same ___.
stages.say: Add today's actual date. Record your chosen technique, what the first test showed, the goal and cue you will keep. You may speak, sign or direct a scribe. I will read your words back. Next lesson we will practise again and keep an honest after test.
stages.good: A dated log links the actual baseline to a small skill goal and a consistent cue for lesson two. Support is recorded and the pupil confirms scribed words.
stages.fallback: Pupil gives an oral or gestured log. Adult records the exact confirmed choice and the observed four-part test at the next available opportunity.
stages.answer: Do not prefill the later result. The after test has not happened yet.

Supported: Choose marks or quiet or silent actions.
Keep four parts in your first test.
Use one adult cue. Practise one small goal.
Tell or show what you noticed for your log.
Independent: Keep a first four-part test. Choose one technique and a small goal.
Use a cue to practise. Keep your first test and a practice record.
Say what stayed the same or changed. Keep the cue for next time.
Aspire: Complete your first test and practice.
Explain why your chosen cue helps the skill.
Say what you will check in the next lesson.
The next level task is optional.

log: Next lesson I will keep ___ the same.
misconceptions: Practice always makes the second version better.
Record what actually happened. It may improve, stay similar or need more practice. A clear observation is useful evidence.
More marks or faster taps show more skill.
The chosen target is control. Keep four marks or actions in the test and focus on the gaps or pace.
A fair before and after comparison can use completely different tasks.
Use the same chosen technique and four-part test. Keep similar conditions and note help. If access requires a new form, keep the old record and make a fresh baseline for that form.
A polished adult example can replace a pupil's first try.
Keep the pupil's real baseline, attempt and words. Label all adult samples as teacher models.
kit: For five pupils: five books or arts logs, five pencils and fifteen small test spaces or sheets for before, practice and after records. Reuse books to avoid extra sheets.

Optional visual route: six drawing tools including the adult model. If using paint, use six brushes, five mats, three stable water pots, a small amount of familiar paint and cloths. Dry marks need no paint.
Quiet or silent route: fingertips or a small comfortable seated action. No instruments or recording device are required.
Adult model: a four-mark line or a four-action pattern, plus a visibly labelled original before and after demonstration. Keep the adult example separate from pupil evidence.
Retain each pupil's chosen technique, baseline and cue for the second period. An adult can make a precise dated observation note when writing materials are unavailable.
demo: 0 to 15 seconds
Show a labelled adult first test with uneven gaps. Say: This is my real starting point for the model. Your before test stays yours.
15 to 30 seconds
Make one small mark, look at its gap, then place a matching mark. Say: I keep one shape and practise its gaps.
30 to 45 seconds
Make a four-action model on one slow count. Say: I keep this cue. I do not make it louder or faster.
45 to 60 seconds
Point to the first test and goal. Say: I will practise, then compare the same four-part test. I cannot promise it will improve today.

stretch.label: Optional next level stretch
stretch.task: Set one skill goal. Keep your first test. Try a cue and ask for one useful comment. Say why you will keep or change the cue for practice. Plan a fair next test.
stretch.evidence: Keep your goal, first test, practice note, feedback and reason. Note the cue for the next test.
stretch.why_optional: This task is extra. Your Explore work is complete without it. Keep the record in case your next level changes.
stretch.good: The pupil links a specific skill target to a chosen practice cue and a reasoned response to feedback. The record sets up a fair later comparison.
stretch.fallback: Adult records the same prompts orally, including the exact four-action sequence, cue, support and pupil's own reason.

models: Teacher model only: My technique is four repeated marks with even gaps. My first row had one small gap. I practised leaving a similar space. I will keep the same mark, size and cue next time.

Teacher model only: My technique is four small actions at a steady pace. I used the same slow count for two practice rounds. I noticed the last action came early. Next time I will practise that final gap.
lessons.cover: Let each pupil choose a four-part mark or quiet or silent action technique. Before modelling, retain a real first test. Model only the chosen feature, then use two short practice rounds with a pause. Keep the baseline, goal, cue and log for lesson two. Use the seven-stage timing and final two Review minutes for tidy-up. No internet, instrument or specialist demonstration is needed.

staff_guidance.plain_language: Resilience can include a pause, a smaller step, asking for help or trying again. Improvement is not guaranteed in one lesson. Notice an honest change, an unchanged feature or a need for more practice.
staff_guidance.scope: Both lessons work at Explore. Complete the core technique practice and arts log without the optional next level task. This week contributes evidence, not a completed award. Retain optional evidence clearly labelled if the owner later reviews the level.
staff_guidance.art_specialist_help: Teach the decision and the method, not a perfect adult performance. Controlled repetition is the focus. Each pupil chooses one technique: four similar marks with roughly even gaps, or four quiet taps or silent finger actions with a steady pace. Keep that same technique across both periods. A pupil can direct an adult or use a smaller movement. Judge a purposeful action and reflection rather than neatness.
staff_guidance.sensory_and_emotional_access: Offer a silent seated route before sound. Use a made-up idea such as calm, a seed growing or a rhythm returning after a pause. No personal disclosure or compulsory public performance. Keep any taps below talking volume and stop on a raised hand. Agree a calm pause and return cue.
staff_guidance.safety: Use familiar non-toxic materials. Clear space for small seated actions. No scissors, pins, recorded media or instruments are required. Keep wet materials on a mat and away from electrical items. Ask before touching a pupil's work. An adult may handle materials under the pupil's direction.
prompt_ladder: Point to the place or instruction.
Model the first step only, then return the task.

adaptations.cognition_and_learning: Teach one technique. Show the four-part test, choose one small target, practise, then repeat the same test. Use a visual or spoken cue and keep it the same for a fair comparison.
adaptations.communication_and_interaction: Accept speech, sign, gesture, a sketch or an adult scribe. Give processing time. Use Before I ... After I ... I notice ... . Read the pupil's words back for confirmation.
adaptations.semh: Let the pupil choose the form and a private audience. Treat a pause or a request for help as part of learning. Avoid rankings, competition and claims that resilience means enduring discomfort.
adaptations.sensory_and_physical: Offer silent finger actions, larger marks, a seated movement or pupil-directed adult action. Choose a comfortable version and retain it for the comparison. Record any change of access or help.
adaptations.eal: Plan in any language. Show repeat, gap and steady using gestures. Check understanding through an action or a labelled sketch before a longer sentence.

staff_guidance.careers_line: Artists and performers practise a specific skill, keep a record and use feedback to plan their next step.

cold_call.middle: What is the one feature you will practise?
cold_call.higher: How will keeping the same cue help your later comparison?

ta_focus.I do: Point to the gap or pace being modelled. Keep the pupil's baseline separate from adult examples.
ta_focus.We do: Use one cue and one target. Model the first step only, then return control.
ta_focus.Independent: Record actual support. Keep baseline, practice and pupil words labelled distinctly.

lessons.evidence: Keep the actual before test made in Starter, a practice record, chosen goal and cue, and dated log. For live actions, a precise witness note is sufficient. No media recording is required. Do not label a practice round as the later after test.
lessons.artist_use_note: This is original technique practice. No reproduced artwork, lyrics or artist quotation is supplied.
lessons.test_conditions: Before the first test, agree a comfortable scale and neutral cue, or no cue. Record the cue and actual access support. Use the same four-part test, similar scale and the same cue and support for the after test. Do not coach the target feature before the baseline.

hinge.question: Our target is even gaps. Which choice helps us practise that skill?

options.A: Change colour and size at once
options.B: Keep the mark and practise its gaps
options.C: Add more marks so the row looks busy

hinge.feedback: B keeps one mark and practises its gaps. Show the feature you will work on.
hinge.wrong_feedback: Keep one feature as the focus. Which option practises the gaps?

lessons.title: My skill before and after
lessons.outcome: Develop a skill and record it in my arts log.
lessons.goal: I can practise the same technique and compare my real before and after tests.
success: I can keep the same technique and test conditions.
I can practise, then keep an honest after test.
I can compare a feature and record my next step.
words: A way of using a skill.
The space or time between two things.
Look or listen for what stayed the same and what changed.

stages.name: Arrival
pupil: Find your before test and chosen technique.
Keep the same four-part test and cue.
stages.say: Find the before test, goal and cue from Monday. We will keep the same technique and a similar size, pace guide and support. If the record is missing, make a fresh dated first test now. Do not invent an earlier result. If access requires a new form, keep the old record and make a new baseline for the new form.
stages.good: The pupil recognises the chosen technique, test and cue. Any missing record, changed help or new access form is noted honestly before a comparison is planned.
stages.fallback: Read back the adult witness note and let the pupil confirm the four-action pattern. If no reliable record exists, observe a fresh baseline today.
stages.answer: Compare only matching tasks. A new baseline can still support useful learning today.

stages.name: Starter
pupil: Point to one feature in your first test.
Say your goal. Do not change the first record.
stages.say: What does the real first test show about gaps or pace? Point to one feature. What was your small goal? We keep the first record exactly as it was so the comparison stays honest.
stages.good: The pupil describes a specific starting feature without altering or improving the baseline. Staff distinguish the pupil's intention from the observed action.
stages.fallback: Pupil confirms one feature from the spoken witness note. Use small gestures or direct the adult to show it.
stages.answer: For example: The gap after mark two was smaller. My last action came sooner. Already steady is also a valid starting observation.

stages.name: I do
pupil: Watch one short practice step.
See the same four-part test before and after.
The after test can stay the same.
stages.say: Here are two real adult model tests using the same mark, size and cue. I compare the gaps, not a new colour or the number of marks. For actions I keep the same four actions and slow cue, then compare their pace. I can say more even, about the same or more varied. I give one feature as my reason.
stages.good: The adult demonstrates a fair comparison of the chosen feature and an honest outcome. The pupil sees that a changed art form or easier test cannot prove the original technique improved.
stages.fallback: Describe two adult four-action examples or perform them silently. Say which feature is being compared. Label adult examples as models.
stages.answer: Check: Which comparison is fair? A four marks before and ten after, B quiet taps before and a picture after, or C the same four-part test with similar conditions? C. If unclear, name the one feature and repeat matching examples.

stages.name: We do
pupil: Try the chosen practice cue once.
Ask for a comment about gaps or pace.
Choose one next practice step.
stages.say: Practise the same technique once. The listener says what they notice about the chosen feature. Hinge: after practice the result looks similar. Should we A pretend it improved, B record what is similar and choose a next step, or C hide the first test? Explain your choice.
stages.good: The pupil selects B and gives a specific next practice action. Feedback describes gaps or pace and leaves the maker in control. The adult models only the first step when needed.
stages.fallback: Use matching silent patterns or pupil-directed adult actions. An adult voices the observed feature and records the pupil's chosen next step.
stages.answer: If A or C is chosen, model an unchanged outcome without blame. Parallel check: If the last action still comes early, can the log say that and plan another try? Yes. Continue when the pupil accepts an honest comparison.

stages.name: Create
pupil: Practise your one technique in two short rounds.
Use the same cue. Pause between rounds.
Make the same four-part after test. Keep both tests.
stages.say: Practise your small goal twice, with a calm pause. Then make the after test: the same four marks or actions, a similar scale or pace guide, the same cue and comparable help. Mark the actual date and label it after. Note any different support. Compare the chosen feature, even if it stayed similar or became less controlled.
stages.good: A real after test follows practice and can be matched to the before record. The pupil identifies a feature, records actual support and gives an honest comparison. Adult help is visible, not presented as independent skill.
stages.fallback: Observe the same four silent actions or pupil-directed adult sequence using the retained cue. Keep a dated witness note of before, after, support and the pupil's explanation. No device is needed.
stages.answer: If form or support must change for access, explain it in the log. A new-form baseline and later matching test can show progress in that form, not a direct improvement claim over the old-form test.

stages.name: Review
pupil: Compare your real before and after tests.
What stayed the same? What changed?
Choose one next step and store the records.
stages.say: Look at or recall the two matching tests. Say one detail about the gaps or pace. It is fine to say unchanged, or that you need more practice. A partner may give a feature-based observation. Use the final two minutes to tidy, cap wet materials, keep work flat and store both tests with the log.
stages.good: The pupil gives a reasoned comparison, accepts a truthful result and chooses a manageable next step. Private sharing is enough. The before and after records remain distinct.
stages.fallback: Adult reads both precise observations aloud. Pupil confirms, corrects or adds their own view. Keep adult observation separate from pupil voice.
stages.answer: Useful: Three gaps look more alike now. The last action still came early. I used more help today. Do not force better as the only valid answer.

stages.name: Exit
pupil: Arts log: Before I ___. After I ___.
I notice ___. My next step is ___.
Say what help you used.
stages.say: Record what the real evidence shows, your view and the support used. You can draw, speak, sign or use a scribe. I will read your words back. Your log shows chosen skill, practice and a before-and-after comparison. The next level task is optional.
stages.good: A dated log links the same technique, two actual tests, practice, a feature-based view, support and next step. No award completion or guaranteed improvement is claimed.
stages.fallback: Pupil confirms an oral or gestured comparison. Adult retains the real ordered tests and exact confirmed words in a dated witness note.
stages.answer: Example only: Before, my final gap was short. After, it was still short. I kept a steady start. Next I will practise the last gap.

Supported: Find your first test and goal with an adult.
Keep the same four-part technique and cue.
Practise, then make a real after test.
Point to one detail. Tell or show your next step.
Independent: Use the same technique and cue. Practise your small goal.
Keep a matching four-part after test.
Compare one feature. Record your view, help and next step.
Aspire: Compare a clear feature in both tests.
Explain how your practice cue helped, or why it did not yet help.
Name one fair next test. The next level task is optional.

log: I used this cue and help ___.
misconceptions: Practice always makes the second version better.
Record what actually happened. It may improve, stay similar or need more practice. A clear observation is useful evidence.
More marks or faster taps show more skill.
The chosen target is control. Keep four marks or actions in the test and focus on the gaps or pace.
A fair before and after comparison can use completely different tasks.
Use the same chosen technique and four-part test. Keep similar conditions and note help. If access requires a new form, keep the old record and make a fresh baseline for that form.
A polished adult example can replace a pupil's first try.
Keep the pupil's real baseline, attempt and words. Label all adult samples as teacher models.
kit: For five pupils: five books or arts logs, five pencils and fifteen small test spaces or sheets for before, practice and after records. Reuse books to avoid extra sheets.

Optional visual route: six drawing tools including the adult model. If using paint, use six brushes, five mats, three stable water pots, a small amount of familiar paint and cloths. Dry marks need no paint.
Quiet or silent route: fingertips or a small comfortable seated action. No instruments or recording device are required.
Adult model: a four-mark line or a four-action pattern, plus a visibly labelled original before and after demonstration. Keep the adult example separate from pupil evidence.
Retain each pupil's chosen technique, baseline and cue for the second period. An adult can make a precise dated observation note when writing materials are unavailable.
demo: 0 to 15 seconds
Show the labelled adult before test. Say: I keep this real starting point and the same four-part task.
15 to 30 seconds
Practise one feature slowly. Say: I keep my mark or action and use the same cue.
30 to 45 seconds
Show an actual matching adult after test. Say: I compare gaps or pace. I do not need to claim it is better.
45 to 60 seconds
Point to a specific feature. Say: This stayed similar. My next step is to practise the final gap. These are adult examples, not your evidence.

stretch.label: Optional next level stretch
stretch.task: Use both tests to review your goal. Say what changed or stayed the same. Explain one comment you used or chose not to use. Set a next goal. Say how you will check it.
stretch.evidence: Keep both tests or witness notes, practice, your view and reasons, feedback and the next goal.
stretch.why_optional: This task is extra. Your Explore work is complete without it. Keep the record in case your next level changes.
stretch.good: The pupil evaluates the chosen technique against their original goal, uses a specific feature as evidence, explains a feedback decision and proposes a fair next check.
stretch.fallback: Adult witnesses the matching live tests and records the same review prompts in the pupil's own confirmed words. No recorded media is required.

models: Teacher model only: My skill was even gaps in four repeated marks. Before, one gap was small. After, the gaps looked more alike. I used the same mark and cue. Next I will try the technique in a short pattern.
Teacher model only: My skill was a steady four-action pace. Before, the last action came early. After, it still came early. The start stayed steady. Next I will practise just the final gap.
lessons.cover: Recover the real baseline, chosen technique, goal and cue. Keep the four-part test comparable. If no trustworthy baseline exists, make a fresh one with today's date before practice. Model a small practice step, allow two short rounds, then retain an honest matching after test and log. Use the same seven-stage timing. Private and silent routes remain valid.

staff_guidance.careers_line: Artists and performers practise a specific skill, keep a record and use feedback to plan their next step.

cold_call.middle: What feature stayed the same or changed?
cold_call.higher: Why is this a fair comparison, and what support must be noted?

ta_focus.I do: Point to the same chosen feature in both model tests. Do not replace the pupil's baseline.
ta_focus.We do: Give feedback about gaps or pace. Accept an unchanged result. Return the choice of next step to the pupil.
ta_focus.Independent: Retain an actual matching after test. Record cue, changed access or support honestly. Scribe exact words and read them back.

lessons.evidence: Keep actual before and after tests of the same chosen technique, the practice record and dated log with a feature-based comparison and support used. Precise witness notes are sufficient for live work. If access changes, retain the original record and establish a new baseline for the new form.
lessons.artist_use_note: This is original technique practice. No reproduced artwork, lyrics or artist quotation is supplied.
lessons.test_conditions: Before the first test, agree a comfortable scale and neutral cue, or no cue. Record the cue and actual access support. Use the same four-part test, similar scale and the same cue and support for the after test. Do not coach the target feature before the baseline.

hinge.question: After practice, the result looks similar. What should we do?

options.B: Record what is similar and choose a next step

hinge.feedback: B keeps the comparison honest. Show one detail and choose a next practice step.
hinge.wrong_feedback: A result can stay similar. Which option records what really happened?

scope: Both pathways work at Explore. Each lesson is complete without the optional GROW next level stretch. Week 2 contributes evidence towards the ongoing arts log and does not by itself complete an award. This is classroom arts learning. No live arts encounter or future event is claimed.
timing: Arrival 0-3; Starter 3-6; I do 6-12; We do 12-18; Create 18-32; Review 32-37; Exit 37-40 minutes. Tidy in the final two minutes of Review.
